title: Yet Another Stone Problem
statementMd:
There are $N$ piles of stones, where the $i$-th pile contains $A_i$ stones. Alice and Bob play a game on these piles. They alternate turns, and Alice moves first. On each turn, the current player must:

1. choose at least $1$ and at most $K$ non-empty piles, and
2. remove a positive number of stones from each chosen pile.

The number of stones removed may differ between the chosen piles. The player who cannot make a move loses. Both players play optimally.

You are given $N$, $K$, $S$ and the name of a player $target$. Construct positive integers $A_1, A_2, \dots, A_N$ such that

- $A_1 + A_2 + \dots + A_N = S$, and
- if the piles initially contain $A_1, A_2, \dots, A_N$ stones, the player named $target$ wins the game.

If no such sequence exists, report it.

## Input

The first line of the input contains an integer $T$ $(1 \le T \le 300)$ denoting the number of test cases. Each of the next $T$ lines contains three integers $N$, $K$, $S$ $(1 \le N \le 10^5$, $1 \le K \le 10^9$, $1 \le S \le 10^{18})$ and a string $target$, which is either $Alice$ or $Bob$.

The sum of $N$ over all test cases does not exceed $5 \cdot 10^5$.

## Output

For each test case, print a single line. If no valid sequence exists, print $-1$. Otherwise, print $N$ positive integers $A_1, A_2, \dots, A_N$ separated by spaces. If there are multiple valid answers, you may print any of them.

## Note

In the first test case, the only possible position is a single pile of $2$ stones. Alice removes both stones in her first move, and Bob cannot move, so Alice wins.

In the second test case, the only possible position is again a single pile of $2$ stones, where Alice wins. So there is no position where Bob wins.

In the third test case, the only possible position is two piles of $1$ stone each. Since $K = 1$, Alice must take one of the piles, Bob takes the other one, and Alice cannot move. So Bob wins.
